fixes.explanation: That's them, friend. The text says "…many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple." Those are the ones who wept. The text doesn't tell us exactly why they wept. I think those tears carried a lot, and I'll leave it at that.
True, friend. The text says the older ones wept loudly. Then it adds, "Still, many others shouted joyfully." So the crowd had both sounds going at once, at the same foundation.

True, friend. The last line says, "And the sound was heard from afar." Verse 13 says the people were making so much noise that no one could tell the shouts of joy from the weeping. That's a sound that carried.

Good instinct, friend. I'd probably order a watchtower too, and a very small helmet for my hat. But no watchtower shows up in this passage. The text says they began to build the altar, and that's what they build.

I can see why you'd pick it, friend. But the text says they feared the people of the land, and it doesn't say they ignored them. Fear and keeping on go together here. They set up the altar and offered the morning and evening burnt offerings all the same.

The Feast of Weeks is a real feast in the Law (Deuteronomy 16:10), but it's not the one this verse names. Ezra 3:4 says they celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles, in accordance with what is written. This all happens in the seventh month, and that's the feast the text gives us.

Not quite, friend. The text says the Israelites began to offer burnt offerings on the first day of the seventh month, "…although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid." So the answer is False. The offerings started first, and the foundation came later.

Right, it's False. The verse says the offerings began "…although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid." So the offerings were already going while the foundation was not yet laid. Offerings first, foundation later.
Sea is right, friend. They gave food and drink and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar logs from Lebanon to Joppa by sea. So the plan was to ship the wood across the water.

A camel is a good thought, but it's not what the verse says. The text says they gave food and drink and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar logs from Lebanon to Joppa by sea. I'd pay good money to see a camel try to carry that load, though, hump and all.

A wagon makes sense if you're picturing a road. But the text says the people of Sidon and Tyre were given food and drink and oil to bring the logs from Lebanon to Joppa by sea. So the route was water, not wheels.

It's actually False, friend. The verse says the cedar logs were to be brought "…as authorized by Cyrus king of Persia." So the Israelites weren't going around the king. They had his go-ahead for the shipment.
Right, False. The logs were to be brought "…as authorized by Cyrus king of Persia." The Israelites weren't going around the king. They had his go-ahead for the shipment.

Tyre does show up in this passage, so I see where that came from. But the text doesn't mention a Hiram. The people of Sidon and Tyre were given food and drink and oil to bring cedar logs, and the supervisors are Levites twenty years of age or older.

Sidon and Tyre are in this passage, but they're the ones given food and drink and oil to bring cedar logs. The weeping comes from the older priests, Levites and family heads who had seen the first temple. The text puts the tears on them.

The people of the land do show up earlier, since the Israelites feared them. But the text doesn't name them among the weepers. It names many of the older priests, Levites and family heads who had seen the first temple, and says they wept loudly.
